narrative:
The model determined that you have a 94.6% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process heavily weighs this predicted outcome, your law school application was rejected.

The strongest factor in this decision was your class ranking at the end of your third year of law school, which placed you in the bottom decile. This was the single most influential piece of information and strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. Your first-year ranking, also in the bottom decile compared to an average of about 6 among accepted students, was the second most important factor and similarly increased the likelihood of failure. Your LSAT score of 36, while only slightly below the 37.18 average of accepted students, was the third most important driver; it worked in the opposite direction and modestly pulled the prediction toward passing.

Taken together, these academic performance signals outweighed other details such as your upper-middle family income, 2.9 undergraduate GPA, and plan to attend full-time. The model concluded that the combination pointed to a high risk of not passing the bar.

You should focus on strengthening your academic record and bar-exam readiness. Consider retaking key courses, seeking targeted tutoring for the bar, or gaining practical legal experience before reapplying. These steps can directly address the areas that most affected your current prediction. (218 words)
